newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ former Auditor-General sent to jail for fraud.
newsitem.headline: NZ former Auditor-General sent to jail for fraud.

text.p: Former Auditor-General and ACC boss Jeff Chapman was on Friday jailed for a total of six months on 10 charges of fraud totalling more than $60,000, the New Zealand Press Association reported.
In the High Court at Wellington, Justice McGechan sentenced Chapman, 58, now of Auckland, to six months' imprisonment on four charges of using a document with intent to defraud.
The charges were that:
* On February 18, 1991, with intent to defraud used a memo seeking an advance of $20,000 towards costs of travel to Indonesia.
* On February 25, 1993, with intent to defraud used a travel agent's invoice to obtain a reimbursement inflated by $6847.
* On May 25, 1993, with intent to defraud used a certified account to obtain a reimbursement of expenses inflated by $20,194.
* On September 5, 1994, with intent to defraud used a note to obtain $US3000 ($NZ4374) travellers cheques.

He was sentenced to three months' in jail on three other charges of making false statements to banks to obtain credit, and on three other charges of using documents with intent to defraud he was convicted and discharged.
All terms were to be served concurrently.
Chapman was found guilty of the 10 charges by Justice McGechan after a three-week trial last month.
The former ACC managing director and Society of Accountants president was acquitted of three other charges, and no verdicts were needed on four which were laid in the alternative.
Earlier in his trial four charges were discharged against Chapman.
Chapman was ACC boss from 1985 to 1992, Society of Accountants president in 1990, and became Auditor-General in December 1992. He had been deputy Auditor-General before going to ACC.
His offending stretched back nearly four years before his resignation from the Audit Office, beginning while he was general manager of ACC.
The crimes carried a maximum of seven years' imprisonment, but the judge said there were mitigating circumstances for a reduced sentence.
These were that the offences were not theft, they were not a long-term scheme to create a nest-egg, Chapman was a first offender, and he was taking steps to pay it back.
Chapman had also had to suffer public disgrace and would never work as a senior employer again, the judge said.
"You have, not to labour the point, fallen a long way and the fall must be a painful one," McGechan said.
"However, I am forced to say this does not suffice, the offending... is just so serious the imposition of any sentence other than imprisonment would be quite inadequate and inappropriate."
He said it was a deliberate fraud and a suspended sentence would not suffice.
Chapman is likely to be given a security classification at either Wellington or Rimutaka prisons.
